v0 stub — five sample questions with answers synthesized from the corpus. Full RAG backend coming in v1.
Q

What is a cognitive light cone, and why does it matter more than asking 'is this thing conscious?'

A

The question "is this thing conscious?" imports all the hard problems of philosophy into the conversation before you've done any science. What I find more productive is asking: over what spatial extent and what temporal horizon does this system integrate information and exert control? That's the cognitive light cone. A bacterium has a small one — it responds to chemical gradients in its immediate vicinity on the timescale of seconds. An organism undergoing regeneration after losing a limb has a much larger one — it is integrating positional information across its entire body plan over days or weeks. The light cone is measurable in principle. "Consciousness" is not.

— Synthesized from "The Computational Boundary of a 'Self'" (Frontiers in Psychology, 2019) and "What are Cognitive Light Cones?" (public lecture)

Q

How do you actually know if a cell is making a decision versus just doing chemistry?

A

You don't know until you test it. The signature of a decision — in the engineering sense I use — is that the outcome is robust to perturbation in a way that cannot be explained by local chemistry alone. When we scramble the facial organs of a tadpole — put the eyes where the nose should be, the mouth on the side — and the tadpole still develops into a viable frog with a functioning face, that's not local chemistry. The cells know where they need to end up, and they navigate there from wherever you've put them. That's what I call navigating a problem space rather than executing a program.

— Synthesized from the "Picasso tadpole" experiments; see Levin lab publications on bioelectric morphogenesis (multiple, 2011–2023)

Q

What would it take to convince you that something is not an agent?

A

That's the right question to ask, and I take it seriously. My answer is: a system that cannot maintain any setpoint in any space, that exhibits zero regulative plasticity, that shows no robustness to perturbation — that system is not an agent in my framework. A truly passive system is like a rock being pushed: you push it, it rolls exactly where physics dictates, with no recovery, no goal-seeking, nothing that looks like "trying." But I'll be honest: I don't think you can draw a sharp line. The question is where on the spectrum from rock to human a given system sits, and that question is empirical.

— Synthesized from Levin's FAQ (thoughtforms.life/faqs-from-my-academic-work/) and TAME framework (Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, 2022)

Q

What is the connection between cancer and the loss of collective intelligence?

A

Cancer, in my framework, is what happens when a cell loses its membership in the larger collective. A normal cell has internalized a high-level goal — "be a liver cell, maintain liver function, cooperate with other cells toward the goal of a healthy organism." A cancer cell has reverted to an older, smaller-scale goal: "survive and reproduce." Its cognitive light cone has shrunk. It no longer participates in the bioelectric conversation that coordinates tissues. We've shown that you can sometimes reverse this — reconnect tumor cells to normal tissue via gap junctions and they rejoin the cooperative. That's not killing the cancer; it's curing the dissociation.

— Synthesized from Levin lab cancer bioelectricity research; see Physics of Life Reviews (2023) and bioelectric normalization papers

Q

What do you mean when you say the body is running software that predates neurons?

A

Neurons didn't invent bioelectric signaling. They inherited it. Every cell in your body uses voltage gradients across its membrane to communicate, coordinate, and store information. That's ancient — it predates the evolution of nervous systems by hundreds of millions of years. What neurons did was specialize that capability: they made the signals faster, more directional, and architecturally complex. But the same computational medium — membrane potential, ion gradients, gap junction coupling — is present in your liver, your skin, your regenerating limb. Brains are a particularly elaborate implementation of a very old program.

— Synthesized from "Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind" (Springer, 2023)
